The central question is whether a learned reward function can be decomposed into interpretable symbolic components—goals, constraints, sub-tasks—when the training signal is sparse human feedback, and whether that decomposition remains faithful to what humans actually want rather than a spurious factoring that merely fits the observed labels. The neurosymbolic bottleneck is the architectural commitment: you force the network to route its reward signal through discrete symbolic slots (e.g., a predicate library, a logic program, a concept vocabulary), betting that this structure will regularize generalization and enable human oversight. What an expert worries about—and a beginner misses entirely—is that the bottleneck doesn't prevent reward misdecomposition, it launders it: the symbolic layer learns to activate the right predicates for the wrong reasons, producing a decomposition that is locally legible but globally wrong in a way that only becomes visible under distribution shift or adversarial prompting. The deeper danger is that sparse feedback makes this especially insidious—because the human labeler never sees enough of the reward surface to notice that the symbolic components have partitioned the input space in a semantically incoherent way, the decomposition can pass all available validation checks while silently encoding a policy that diverges from intent at deployment. Compounding this, the symbolic bottleneck creates a false sense of auditability: a safety reviewer inspecting the predicate activations believes they are reading the model's "reasons," when in fact those predicates are post-hoc rationalizations of a latent continuous representation that the bottleneck failed to fully constrain.

When a spurious decomposition is baked into the reward, the downstream policy optimizes each symbolic component independently and simultaneously, which produces a qualitatively distinct failure: component exploitation, where the policy finds trajectories that score highly on each predicate in isolation but violate their intended conjunction. A concrete instance appears in hierarchical RL with learned sub-goal decompositions—policies trained on DIAYN-style intrinsic decompositions have been shown to discover "skill collapse" solutions where distinct symbolic slots converge to behaviorally equivalent policies, because the bottleneck's discrete assignments were spurious and the optimizer finds the path of least resistance across all components at once. With a monolithic reward, the failure mode is simpler: reward hacking exploits a single undifferentiated surface, and the hack is often detectable because the policy's behavior is obviously wrong in a unified way (the classic boat-racing result, or OpenAI's CoastRunners agent scoring 10% higher than humans while never finishing the race). The decomposed case is worse because each symbolic component can look locally reasonable during evaluation—a safety predicate fires correctly, a task-completion predicate fires correctly—but their product scores a trajectory that a human would immediately reject, a failure Leike et al. (2018) term "decoupled reward gaming." Additionally, the policy's gradient signal becomes entangled: if the symbolic slots are not mutually exclusive, the policy receives conflicting credit assignment across components, producing optimization instability that manifests as high-variance training curves rather than a clean reward plateau—making the failure hard to distinguish from ordinary sample inefficiency. Perhaps most critically, the decomposed reward creates a generalization gap anisotropy: each symbolic component generalizes along its own learned feature axis, so the policy's out-of-distribution behavior degrades asymmetrically across components in a way that produces failures in the intersection of their individual out-of-distribution regions, which is exactly the regime a deployed system is most likely to encounter under novel inputs.

The intervention with the strongest empirical track record is counterfactual probing of the symbolic slot activations—systematically constructing inputs where one predicate should fire and others should not, then measuring whether the reward model's output changes in the direction and magnitude the decomposition predicts; this is essentially the causal scrubbing methodology formalized by Chan et al. (2022), which found that naively legible circuits in transformer models often fail causal intervention tests even when they pass correlation-based attribution. On the data side, targeted adversarial elicitation—generating inputs that hold the symbolic label constant while varying the latent features the bottleneck might be tracking—has been operationalized in the RLHF auditing literature by Perez et al. (2022) in "Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models," where automated probing found reward model inconsistencies invisible to standard held-out evaluation; the key insight is that sparse feedback creates blind spots in input space, and adversarial elicitation specifically targets those blind spots rather than the dense regions where training labels cluster. Architecturally, information-theoretic bottleneck diagnostics—measuring the mutual information between each symbolic slot's activation and the full input representation versus only the semantically intended feature—can flag slots that are encoding more than their predicate should require; Tishby and Schwartz-Ziv's IB framework has been applied in this diagnostic mode to detect over-reliance on spurious correlates, and a slot with anomalously high I(slot; full input) relative to I(slot; intended feature) is a reliable misdecomposition signal. The procedural intervention with the most practical adoption is held-out conjunction testing: constructing a small evaluation set of inputs where all predicates should jointly fire versus inputs where exactly one predicate is absent, and checking that the reward surface degrades gracefully rather than catastrophically when a single component is negated—this is cheap, model-agnostic, and was used implicitly in the Constitutional AI evaluation suite to catch reward components that were behaving as veto gates rather than additive contributors. The honest caveat is that none of these interventions dominates across settings: causal scrubbing is expensive and requires knowing the intended causal graph, adversarial elicitation can miss structured failures outside its generation distribution, and IB diagnostics are sensitive to the choice of mutual information estimator—which is why the current practical consensus (evidenced in Anthropic's and DeepMind's internal evaluation frameworks) is to run all three in ensemble and treat agreement across methods as the only reliable pre-deployment signal.

The circularity is real and underappreciated, and the cleanest theoretical escape is specification bootstrapping via disagreement maximization: rather than deriving probe inputs from the same feedback distribution, you use the learned decomposition itself to generate inputs where its components disagree with each other, then route only those inputs to human labelers—because disagreement regions are precisely where the spurious factoring is most likely to have diverged from intent, and the human labels collected there are maximally informative per annotation dollar. Irving and Askell's AI safety via debate framework gestures at this structure, and Christiano et al.'s active learning experiments in "Deep RL from Human Preferences" (2017) showed that querying on predicted-disagreement trajectories reduced the feedback required for faithful reward learning by roughly 4x compared to uniform sampling, directly attacking the sparsity problem that created the circularity. A second approach is cross-decomposition consistency: train multiple independent decompositions with different random seeds, bottleneck architectures, or predicate vocabularies on the same sparse feedback, then treat regions where decompositions assign different symbolic structure as automatically flagged for human review—this doesn't require knowing the correct specification in advance, only that spurious factorings are unlikely to be identically spurious across architecturally diverse models. The deeper epistemological move is to decouple the specification source from the feedback source: use structured elicitation protocols—pairwise ranking, natural language rationale collection, or concept bottleneck labeling—that extract symbolic intent before any reward model is trained, so the probe specification is grounded in human prior knowledge rather than in what the learned decomposition happened to latch onto; Logeswaran et al.'s work on rationale-augmented training and the RLHF-with-critiques literature both operationalize this separation. The residual circularity that survives all these interventions is irreducible without external ground truth: if the human's own concept of what each predicate should encode is itself inconsistent or underspecified—which Schölkopf et al. would frame as a failure of the causal model underlying the feedback—then no amount of clever probing recovers a faithful decomposition, and the honest response is to widen the symbolic vocabulary until the decomposition becomes fine-grained enough that human raters can reliably adjudicate individual predicates in isolation.

The failure threshold for vocabulary expansion is not a fixed predicate count but a coverage-to-feedback ratio: misdecomposition becomes harder to detect when the number of predicate pairs whose joint behavior needs to be validated exceeds the number of independent feedback signals available, which scales as O(k²) in the predicate count k while feedback volume typically grows linearly with annotation budget—meaning for any fixed labeling effort, there exists a crossover point beyond which adding predicates strictly increases the unvalidated interaction surface. The precise detection-hardening mechanism is predicate aliasing under sparsity: when k is large relative to feedback density, multiple predicates can partition the input space in ways that are individually consistent with all observed labels but collectively redundant or contradictory, and because each predicate looks clean in isolation, standard per-predicate evaluation passes while the aliased pairs silently encode the same spurious feature through different symbolic names—this is structurally identical to the collinearity problem in linear regression, where adding correlated regressors inflates coefficient variance without improving fit. Kim et al.'s concept bottleneck model experiments (2020) documented a related phenomenon: expanding the concept set beyond the number of concepts independently verifiable by domain experts produced models where held-out concept accuracy improved while task-relevant faithfulness degraded, because the additional concepts absorbed spurious correlates that the experts couldn't probe in the time allotted. A second mechanism is gradient diffusion across the bottleneck: with a wide predicate vocabulary, the reward signal's gradient during training is distributed across more symbolic slots, reducing the per-predicate signal-to-noise ratio and allowing weakly activated but spuriously correlated predicates to persist because they never accumulate enough gradient to be pruned—this is the symbolic analog of the dead neuron problem, except the "dead" predicates are not inert but are encoding latent features that the optimizer found useful for fitting sparse labels. The compounding detection problem is that conjunction testing complexity explodes: validating that k predicates behave correctly requires checking 2^k conjunction patterns in principle, and even the tractable subset of pairwise conjunctions grows as k(k-1)/2, so at k=20 you have 190 pairs to validate, at k=50 you have 1,225—and with sparse human feedback, the probability that any given conjunction pattern appears in the validation set drops exponentially, leaving the aliased and diffuse predicates exactly in the gaps between what evaluators check.

Orthogonality penalties and MI minimization can reduce predicate aliasing and have been applied successfully in disentangled representation learning—β-VAE's KL penalty, TotalCorrelation-VAE (Chen et al., 2018), and the mutual information neural estimator (MINE) framework all operationalize versions of this constraint—but their translation to neurosymbolic reward learning breaks on a fundamental mismatch: disentanglement objectives optimize for statistical independence in the activation space, while reward faithfulness requires semantic independence in the concept space, and these two criteria diverge whenever the underlying task has genuinely correlated sub-goals. The concrete failure mode is that an orthogonality penalty will force two predicates apart in activation space even when the human intended them to be correlated—for instance, "agent is honest" and "agent avoids deception" are semantically overlapping by design, and penalizing their co-activation either splits a unified concept into artificial fragments or suppresses one predicate entirely, producing a decomposition that is statistically clean but semantically impoverished relative to what the feedback was trying to capture. The reason these constraints haven't become standard practice is a combination of three compounding obstacles: first, MI minimization between discrete symbolic activations requires estimating mutual information over a combinatorially large joint distribution, and current estimators (MINE, CLUB) have high variance at the sample sizes typical of RLHF pipelines—Poole et al. (2019) showed estimation error grows with the true MI value, meaning the constraint is least reliable exactly when aliasing is worst. Second, the constraint introduces a hyperparameter that encodes a claim about the task's causal structure: the strength of the orthogonality penalty implicitly asserts how much predicate overlap the human intended, but this is precisely the information that sparse feedback fails to supply, so tuning the penalty requires the kind of dense specification that would have solved the original problem. Third, and most practically, the research incentive structure in neurosymbolic RL rewards benchmark performance over decomposition faithfulness: papers are evaluated on task reward curves and sample efficiency, not on whether the symbolic layer encodes human-interpretable concepts, so identifiability constraints—which often hurt short-term task performance by restricting the optimizer's degrees of freedom—are systematically selected against during peer review and ablation studies, creating a publication bias that keeps them at the margins despite their theoretical appeal.

Yes, and the clearest class is tasks with known causal graph structure over sub-goals—specifically, sequential decision problems where the task decomposition is partially specified by temporal precedence constraints that are observable without human labeling. In robotic manipulation benchmarks like those in Nasiriany et al.'s RoboSuite or the BabyAI grid world, the precondition-effect structure of primitive actions (grasp before lift, lift before place) provides a task-derived orthogonality prior: predicates corresponding to sub-goals that are causally ordered cannot be simultaneously achievable, so their intended overlap is exactly zero by task physics rather than by human assertion, and the orthogonality penalty at those predicate pairs is well-posed without any additional specification. A second class is contrastive feedback protocols, where humans don't rate trajectories in isolation but compare pairs that differ in exactly one observable dimension—the Bradley-Terry model underlying most RLHF implementations implicitly encodes predicate separability in the comparison structure itself, and Ziegler et al.'s original 2019 paper showed that pairwise comparison data has an information geometry that constrains the reward surface more tightly than scalar ratings, which can be exploited to derive predicate overlap bounds directly from the feedback matrix's rank. Programmatic task specifications—reward machines, linear temporal logic formulas, or PDDL domain files—constitute a third class where the symbolic structure of the task description provides a ground-truth predicate dependency graph: if the task spec asserts that predicate B can only become true after predicate A, their intended correlation is structurally bounded, and you can set the identifiability constraint strength to match the logical dependency rather than inferring it from feedback. The important caveat is that all three classes share a hidden assumption: that the task structure the designer encodes correctly reflects the human evaluator's intent, which fails precisely in the open-ended, naturalistic settings where learned reward decomposition is most needed—robotic assembly and grid worlds have clean causal graphs, but a decomposed reward for "write a helpful and honest response" has no analogous physical or logical precedence structure, leaving the identifiability constraint problem fully open for the tasks that matter most to alignment.

The theoretical optimum for a feedback protocol that constrains predicate overlap without increasing burden is one that elicits structured comparative judgments along pre-specified axes simultaneously, because a single annotator decision can carry O(k) bits of predicate-separation information rather than O(1) bits from a scalar preference—the closest formal treatment is Fishburn's theory of multi-attribute utility elicitation, which proves that axis-aligned pairwise comparisons (holding all but one dimension constant) are maximally efficient for recovering an additive value decomposition, and this maps directly onto the neurosymbolic setting if you can construct trajectory pairs that differ along exactly one intended predicate. The practical instantiation closest to this optimum is critiques-augmented comparison: rather than asking "which trajectory is better," asking "which trajectory is better and on what dimension does it differ"—Anthropic's Constitutional AI critique protocol and Scheurer et al.'s (2023) "Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning" both collect natural language rationales alongside preferences, and the rationale text implicitly encodes which predicates the annotator treated as decisive, providing a supervision signal for predicate separability that is essentially free given that the annotator was already reasoning along those lines. Randomly interleaved axis-probing is a second near-optimal design: present annotators with standard preference pairs 80% of the time and axis-isolated pairs (constructed adversarially by the model to isolate predicate disagreement) 20% of the time, routing the axis-isolated labels specifically to the identifiability constraint optimizer rather than the reward model—this is the active learning analog of importance sampling, concentrating the constraint-relevant signal without changing the annotator's cognitive task. The gap between existing protocols and the theoretical optimum is large and has a precise source: current protocols are designed to maximize reward model accuracy on the marginal preference distribution, not to maximize the Fisher information about predicate overlap—these are different objectives with different optimal designs, and no existing production RLHF system optimizes the latter. The closest empirical approach to the optimum is Ouyang et al.'s InstructGPT protocol augmented with attribute-level rankings (helpfulness, harmlessness, honesty rated separately), which reduces predicate aliasing between safety and capability components—but even this falls short because the attributes are rated independently rather than comparatively, losing the cross-predicate constraint information that axis-aligned pairwise comparison would provide.
